lawyer:
Shah Khashruzzaman with Reshma Sultana, Advocates ------ For the Applicant. 
Kazi Waliul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General ------ For the Respondent.
parties:
Anil Chandra Paul ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Commissioner of Taxes  ------ Respondent
full_judgment: 9. Mr Shah Khashruzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing for the assessee applicant, submits that section 93 of Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 clearly provides that the Department must have definite information about the income before re-opening the case. But in this case the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes had no definite information before him that the assessee applicant is found to be the owner of the said amount of money and, as such, obtaining approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes before re-opening the assessment of the assessee applicant is not in accordance with law. He further submits that from the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, it clearly appears that on the direction of the National Board of Revenue by its letter dated 15-11-2001 and also on the basis of the Commissioner's letter dated 20-11-2001, the case has been re-opened on 29-12-2001 without having any definite information in his hand. He also submits that the Bank statement and other papers were filed subsequent to re-opening of the case and, as such, the entire re-assessment proceeding under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance is unwarranted, illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction. He further submits that the Bank statement clearly shows that the amount remitted to the assessee applicant's account in the concerned financial year is Taka 6,05,00,000 (Taka six crore five lac), not Taka 5,40,00,000 (Taka five crore forty lac) but the National Board of Revenue as well as the Commissioner of Taxes directed the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to re-open the case of the assessee applicant for unexplained account of raka 5,40,00,000 (Taka five crore forty lac), which s very much incorrect, clearly proves that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes had no definite information for which the case could be re-opened under section 93. In fact, the Department without holding proper investigation in the matter re-opened the file of the assessee applicant and arbitrarily assessed Taka 5,40,00,000 (Taka five crore forty lac) as income from other sources under section 19(5) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. Moreover the said amount admittedly was not in existence on 30-6-2000 in the account of the assessee-applicant, only Taka 2,54,496.37 (Taka two lac fifty-four thousand four hundred ninety-six and third-seven paisa) was shown in the statement of the Bank not Taka 5,40,00,000 (Taka five crore forty lac) and therefore, the same cannot be treated as in assessee applicant's possession and, as such, in this case, section 19(5) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 cannot be attracted. In support of his contention Mr Zaman relied on the case of JK Synthetics Ltd. and others vs Central Board of District Taxes and others reported in ITR Vol. 83(SC) 1972 page 335 and he also submits that after re-opening of the said assessment, the information as to the names and addresses of the remitters were supplied by the assessee-applicant and it is admitted that ten letters out of the twelve letters have duly been served upon the remitters which proved that the remitters were not fictitious persons and, as such, the initial onus of burden of proof of the assessee-applicant is discharged. But the Department without investigating the matter, in accordance with law, came to a wrong conclusion that the assessee-applicant has failed to prove his case by filing documentary evidences. He further submits that the Department, upon receipt of the information as to the particulars of the remitters concerned, should have investigated the matter through proper channel by issuing notices upon the remitters under the provision of section 6 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 otherwise the remitters are not duty bound to comply with the notices issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Circle-18, Taxes Zone-3, Chittagong as they are not the assessees of Chittagong Zone. He also submits that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes should have forwarded the subsequent notices through the Commissioner of Taxes, Chittagong Zone-3, Chittagong for onward communication of notices to the Commissioner of Taxes of the respective Zone which the concerned Deputy Commissioner of Taxes have not complied with and in that way the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes travelled beyond his jurisdiction as notified in the Office Order No. lE-40/91-92 dated 2-5-1992 of the Commissioner of Taxes, Taxes Zone-3, Chittagong. In support of his contention he relied on the case of Orient Trading Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of income Tax Central (Calcutta) reported in ITR (1963) Vol. 49 page 723 and Udhavdas Kewalram vs Commissioner of income T!:a, Bombay reported in ITR (1967) Bombay Vol. 66, page 462. He also submits that the Department as per section 117 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 to verify the remittance register to ascertain from where the remittances were issued and this section has also provided the detailed mode of search and seizure which has not been complied with, on the contrary, it has added the amount of Taka 5,40,00,000 (Taka five crore forty lac) with the income of the assessee- applicant without any evidence on record.
